html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Use a symptom-to-layer method and the core kubectl tools
  • Read Pod states such as Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff and OOMKilled
  • Diagnose a Service with no endpoints, DNS failures and a NotReady node
  • Recognize quota and RBAC denials, and find component logs

2The symptom-to-layer method and the kubectl tools (get, describe, events, logs, exec, debug, top)

Running case

Harbor Books Has a Bad Morning

  • A new orders Pod stays Pending, and nobody knows why
  • The storefront cannot reach catalog, although the catalog Pods are running
  • One worker node reports NotReady, and a developer's request is rejected as Forbidden
  • In this module you find which layer is at fault

A Symptom-to-Layer Method

  • Start with triage: is the problem in the Pod, in its controller or in the Service?
  • Read the symptom, then name the layer: scheduling, container, network, storage, node or access
  • Inspect that layer with describe, events and logs
  • Change one thing at a time, and check that the symptom is gone

Exam tip: Symptom first, then the layer, then the matching command.

kubectl Tools for Troubleshooting

  • get shows the state and the restarts; describe ends with the events
  • logs --previous shows the log of the crashed container
  • exec runs a command or opens a shell inside a container; debug adds an ephemeral container
  • top shows CPU and memory use, when the Metrics Server is installed

Look, ask why, read the logs, step inside

kubectl get pods -n shop
kubectl describe pod orders -n shop
kubectl get events -n shop
kubectl logs orders --previous
kubectl exec -it orders -- sh
kubectl top pod -n shop

Exam tip: describe says why; logs say what the application printed.

3Pod states (Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, Evicted, Terminating) and Pending in detail

Pod States and What They Mean

State What it means First check
Pending accepted, but not placed on a node yet the events in describe
ImagePullBackOff the image cannot be pulled; retries with a growing delay image name, registry, imagePullSecret
CrashLoopBackOff the container keeps failing and restarting logs --previous and the configuration
OOMKilled the container used more memory than its limit memory use, a leak, or a higher limit
Evicted the kubelet ended the Pod under node pressure free resources on the node
Terminating a deletion was issued but cannot finish finalizers and admission webhooks

Exam tip: Pending is about placement; the BackOff states are about the container.

Pending in Detail

  • Pending means the Pod is accepted but not placed; describe shows the scheduler's reason
  • Resources: not enough CPU or memory for its requests, so free resources, lower the requests or add nodes
  • Placement: selectors, affinity or taints match no node (Module 5), or a hostPort limits where it can go
  • Storage: a claim (PVC) that cannot bind keeps the Pod from being placed (Module 7)

Exam tip: Pending: read the events first.

4Node NotReady, the kubelet, control plane and node logs, what the exam asks

NotReady Nodes and Component Logs

  • A node that is down, cut off, or has a dead kubelet shows NotReady
  • The node controller sets Ready to Unknown, and by default evicts its Pods after 5 minutes
  • kubectl get nodes and kubectl describe node show the condition and the events
  • Logs: kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager on the control plane; kubelet and kube-proxy on workers
  • On systemd hosts the kubelet and runtime write to journald: use journalctl

Exam tip: NotReady: look at the node and its kubelet.

What the Exam Asks: Troubleshooting

  • Pending or ImagePullBackOff: not placed yet, or placed but the image cannot be pulled
  • CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled: the container keeps failing, or it hit its memory limit
  • describe or logs: events and state, or what the application printed; --previous for a crashed container
  • No endpoints: the selector and the Pod labels do not match
  • NotReady: the node or its kubelet; Pods are evicted after 5 minutes by default
  • Forbidden: RBAC or a quota, not a cluster fault

Exam tip: Name the layer before you pick a command.

5A Service with no endpoints, DNS failures

A Service With No Endpoints, and DNS Failures

  • Check in order: does the Service exist, does its name resolve, does it have EndpointSlices
  • No endpoints points to a selector that matches no Pods; compare it with the Pods' labels
  • The Pod's containerPort must match the Service's targetPort
  • DNS: run nslookup from a Pod, and check that the CoreDNS Pods, labeled k8s-app=kube-dns, are running
  • Then look at kube-proxy and any NetworkPolicy

Exam tip: No endpoints: compare the selector with the Pod labels.

6Quota and RBAC denials

Quota and RBAC Denials

Rejection Cause Check
Forbidden (403) from RBAC no role grants the action to that user or ServiceAccount kubectl auth can-i, then the roles and bindings
Forbidden (403) from a quota the request would break a ResourceQuota, and the message names the constraint kubectl describe quota in the namespace
  • Both come from the control plane, and they are policy answers: the cluster is healthy
  • With quotas on for CPU or memory, a Pod must state requests or limits, or it is rejected

Exam tip: A 403 is a policy answer, not a broken cluster.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1A container keeps crashing and restarting. Which command shows the log of its previous, crashed instance?

  • Akubectl top pod orders, which shows the CPU and memory use of the Pod
  • Bkubectl logs orders --previous, which prints the log of the earlier container
  • Ckubectl get events, which lists recent events for the namespace of the Pod
  • Dkubectl describe node, which shows the conditions of the node that runs the Pod
Show the answer

Answer: B. The previous option of the logs command shows the log of the container that crashed. Top shows resource use, events and describe show state changes but not the application's output.

S2A new Harbor Books orders Pod stays Pending, and describe shows that no node has enough free CPU for its requests. Which actions can fix this?

  • ALower the CPU requests of the Pod, free resources on the nodes, or add nodes
  • BDelete the Service of the orders Pods, so that the scheduler can start again
  • CRestart the kubelet on every control plane node, so that the Pod is placed
  • DRaise the memory limit of the container, because Pending means too little memory
Show the answer

Answer: A. Pending means the Pod is not placed, and here the reason is CPU requests that no node can satisfy. Lowering requests, freeing resources or adding nodes addresses that. A Service, a control plane kubelet and a memory limit have nothing to do with it.

S3A worker node shows NotReady in kubectl get nodes. Which cause is likely?

  • AToo many labels have been added to the node, so the scheduler refuses to use it
  • BThe Deployments that run on the node have more replicas than the cluster allows
  • CThe Service selectors of the cluster do not match the Pods that run on the node
  • DThe kubelet on the node has stopped, or the node has lost contact with the control plane
Show the answer

Answer: D. A node that stops reporting, because it is down, cut off or its kubelet died, gets the Ready condition Unknown and shows NotReady. Labels, replica counts and Service selectors do not make a node NotReady.

S4The Harbor Books storefront cannot reach catalog through its Service. The EndpointSlices of the Service list no addresses, yet the catalog Pods are Running. What is the likely cause?

  • AThe CoreDNS Pods are not running, so the Service name is not resolved
  • BThe nodes that run the catalog Pods are NotReady, so the Pods do not respond
  • CThe selector of the Service does not match the labels of the catalog Pods
  • DThe Service is of type ClusterIP, which does not get EndpointSlices
Show the answer

Answer: C. EndpointSlices list the Pods that match the Service selector, so an empty list with running Pods points to a selector or label mismatch. A DNS failure would break name resolution, not the endpoint list, and ClusterIP Services do have EndpointSlices.

S5A request to create more Pods in a namespace is rejected with 403 Forbidden, and the message says a quota would be exceeded. Which statement is correct?

  • AThe kubelet evicted the Pods of the namespace because the node ran short of resources
  • BThe control plane rejected the request because it would break the ResourceQuota of the namespace
  • CRBAC denied the request, because the user has no role in the namespace at all
  • DThe kube-proxy blocked the request, because the Service has too many endpoints
Show the answer

Answer: B. A request that would violate a ResourceQuota is rejected by the control plane with 403 Forbidden and a message naming the constraint. It is a policy answer, not an eviction, an RBAC denial or a proxy problem.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Method symptom, layer, inspect, fix one thing, verify
Tools get, describe, events, logs with --previous, exec, debug, top
Pod states Pending is placement; ImagePullBackOff is the image; CrashLoopBackOff is the container; OOMKilled is the memory limit
Pending resources, placement rules or a claim that cannot bind
Cluster a NotReady node means a dead kubelet or network; read the component logs
Services and access no endpoints is a selector mismatch; 403 is RBAC or a quota
